children: Indian companies stepped up acquisitions overseas in 2026 even as overall dealmaking slowed, with outbound M&A value jumping 76 per cent to $8.8 billion in the first seven months of the year from $5 billion a year earlier, according to a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) report.
The increase came despite the number of outbound transactions falling 19 per cent to 92, indicating that Indian companies were spending more on fewer overseas acquisitions.
Meanwhile, inbound deal value, involving foreign buyers acquiring Indian companies, fell 58 per cent to $2.7 billion, while domestic M&A value declined 14 per cent to $10.1 billion.

The rise in overseas acquisitions helped cushion the broader slowdown in the Indian M&A market. Overall deal volumes fell about 20 per cent during January-July, slightly more than the 18 per cent decline globally, but transaction value was down only 2 per cent as companies continued to pursue larger deals. India’s deal activity also remained above pre-pandemic levels despite the decline.

“The Indian outbound story isn’t just the large conglomerates anymore – we are seeing mid-sized companies buy capabilities and market access abroad, and that is a healthy sign of confidence,” said Dhruv Shah, Managing Director and Partner at BCG.

BCG said Indian companies are looking overseas for three broad reasons to expand supply chains in industries where they already compete globally, gain access to customers and order books in developed markets, and acquire capabilities that are difficult to build or source domestically.

The last of these is particularly visible in technology, where Indian IT services companies are buying overseas businesses with AI capabilities. Acquisitions by Coforge and Infosys among examples of companies choosing to acquire such capabilities rather than build them entirely in-house.

The overall slowdown in deal volumes, meanwhile, reflects greater selectivity rather than a shortage of capital, the report said. Rich public-market valuations have widened the gap between buyers' and sellers' expectations, while tariff and geopolitical uncertainty and currency depreciation have also made companies more cautious. India-focused financial sponsors still have more than $20 billion of dry powder, according to Preqin data cited by BCG.

The deals that are going through are also getting a better reception from investors. M&A announcements by listed Indian companies generated a median 30-day relative shareholder return of 3.7 per cent in 2026, against minus 0.4 per cent in 2024 and minus 2.7 per cent in 2025.
“Volumes have fallen while the market is rewarding those that still transact with conviction,” said Kanchan Samtani, APAC Leader, Corporate Finance & Strategy, MD and Senior Partner at BCG.

title: Indian companies step up overseas M&As as domestic dealmaking slows
